scholarship.title: Anunna (Anunnaku, Anunnaki): a group of gods
scholarship.author: Nicole Brisch
scholarship.summary: ORACC's scholarly overview describes a changing collective term: high gods or a local pantheon in Sumerian evidence, and sometimes underworld gods in later evidence. Membership and number vary by period and context.

scholarship.title: Igigi / Igigu and the Anunna
scholarship.author: Nicole Brisch
scholarship.summary: The relationship between Igigi and Anunna is historically variable and not fully resolved; the labels should not be flattened into one timeless roster.

alternatives.title: Scope of the collective
alternatives.summary: Attested uses can denote leading gods broadly or the pantheon of a particular city. The cited overview says the exact membership is unclear.

alternatives.title: Later underworld emphasis
alternatives.summary: Later Akkadian usage can emphasize underworld gods in contrast with the Igigi, while earlier Sumerian uses are not restricted to that role.

modernClaims.title: Anunnaki as visitors from Nibiru
modernClaims.summary: The publisher presents Sitchin's modern claim that the Anunnaki came from a planet called Nibiru and periodically landed on Earth.
modernClaims.evidence: Primary source for the modern claim; not evidence about antiquity

modernClaims.title: Anunnaki creation of human workers
modernClaims.summary: The publisher attributes to Sitchin the hypothesis that Enki created humanity as a primitive worker for extraterrestrial Anunnaki.
modernClaims.evidence: Primary source for the modern claim; not evidence about antiquity

comparisons.ancientRecord: The cited ORACC lines attest the divine-name spelling in Sumerian compositions; ORACC's scholarly overview treats Anunna/Anunnaki as a group of deities whose scope changes by context.
comparisons.finding: The cited ancient evidence and scholarly overview do not identify the group as extraterrestrial visitors or name Nibiru as their home.
comparisons.limitation: This comparison is bounded to the cited lines and overview; it is not a claim that every surviving Mesopotamian text has been exhaustively searched.

comparisons.ancientRecord: The name occurs in different literary settings, and the scholarly overview warns that membership, number and function vary across periods.
comparisons.finding: The source record supports a variable divine collective, not a single fixed biological population described by modern racial or technological terms.
comparisons.limitation: A transliteration attestation alone does not settle translation, theology or historical development.

comparisons.ancientRecord: The cited line is retained as untranslated Sumerian composite evidence; Atlas does not supply a meaning beyond the attested divine-name form.
comparisons.finding: Nothing in this cited line establishes extraterrestrial genetic engineering or gold-mining labor.
comparisons.limitation: Other creation traditions require their own editions and philological analysis; absence from one line is not universal negative proof.
